title: Clarinet lessons, ukulele, the Boozan Kings and first banjo jobs
summary: From lessons through the ukulele and his boy band to his first banjo jobs, including Billy Phillips and Lee Collins, Barker tells his start in a single long answer.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: He played with the Arnold Brass Band. They played first clarinet. He died young with a social disease. My great-aunt term. He was a shy boy. He was a basketball sergeant. Some sportswoman enticed him and got in a corral and contacted his disease. And they wouldn't tell the old folks that he was sick. And somehow they detected that he had this trouble. And when they found out about it and rushed him to the hospital, it was too late. So he died of this sickness. And this is just a lot on the planet. So Michael Paul came back to Chicago in 1921. And then Chicago King Holland came back there with a planet. And he suggested I take some lessons. I think it was 1923. And he had a planet, so I take a half a dozen lessons to the planet with Bonabee God. And he was a big one in the big garden. But I didn't know I didn't care too much about it. And I wanted to blow something right away. And they were just trying to show me the notes. Tell me to the client at home, come get the notes for us, you know, with the reading one. So I just drifted off from it. Didn't play it, paid no mind. So in 1924, Mapa Paul's sister Teresa bought a ukulele. It was a ukulele craze. She bought a banjo-yuk. She tried it for a while and she left it around the house. So I started playing fool around with it. She didn't mind. And I started acting like it was mine. So she said, uh, where's my ukulele? I said, it's home. She said, well, it don't belong to you. I said, well, would you sell it to me? She said, yeah, how much do you want to pay? She said, well, I paid seven dollars for it. I said, well, I'll pay you on that installment plan. She said, no. She said, I'll tell you, give me one dollar and you can have it. So I gave my dollar for it. And I didn't know how to tune it. There was a boy around the corner from my house named Ashton Murray, who was a piano player. Now schoolteacher in New Orleans. Well-bred boy. Yeah. Nice family. I'd knock on his door every evening and ask him to tune it for me. And he tuned the ukulele from me. To get out of tune, I'd go back and ask him again. So finally he told me to listen to the tone of the strings. from me. And he tuned the ukulele from me. When you get out of tune, I'd go back and ask him again. So finally he told me to listen up to the tone of the strings. And I could line the tunes like that and start singing. I learned to tune it. I didn't worry asking him anymore. So I started playing the ukulele. And I organized a little, I started a little tramp band, I was called a pickin' in a band. A little guy made up of a little jive set of drums and a washboard and a little contraption. You'll see him run, I know his kids make them a kazoo prayer. Another guy, a little makeshift tambourine, four of us. Remember their names? I called a group of Boozan Kings. The what? The Boozan Kings. B-O-O-Z-A-N. Boozan. Boozan means good time in Patois from some angle of it. It was a very popular word. They said I'm going over to someone, so they're having a Boozan over there. Or they're having a ball, or they're having a parlor. But the boys at the same time, they said, man, they're going to have a Boozan, so it's some person else. So, we got to a little group I had, we used to sneak off in the district. After seven o'clock at night, we'd go in the ballroom. I'd go and ask the bartender, can we play a couple of tunes? Can we play some tunes? Got Lil Liza, and Jan, and My Blue Heaven, and all the current songs we'd sing. We'd pass the hat around. In other words, we'd hustle. So, the group got popular, we'd play on the steps, and all the kids in the school, as I call them, and all the kids in the neighborhood would kind of get around us. We'd be balling in the afternoon, you know, after school. We'd have to have our rehearsals in the street. And it was nice things, you know, combat juvenile delinquency. So, we had a little, we organized a little club, about seventeen or eighteen members, and we'd start giving parties. And then people, the other kids in the seven ward was, would hire a little group to play for their parties, because they became very popular. And I became very good on the ukulele. So, like, old man's like, old, the old man like, Emil Glenny, Walter DeCouw, big-eyed lawyer. They used to see me with this ukulele. Emil Glenny? What did Emil, uh, uh, Alvin? Yeah. I said Emil Glenny, because he's a little nephew, Emil playing with me. Oh, yeah. He played the tambour. Oh, yeah. I trained him out of passing the cat around with a very sad expression on his face. Well, then, what happened, that, I've been playing two or three different keys, I don't know if you can play the ukulele or four different keys. And every time I'd go to the party, I'd stand around the banjo and the kids would tell me, say, get your banjo, you can play that ukulele or betterness cat for whoever else was in the band playing the banjo, you know. So, I got this idea in my head. I didn't pay it to my mind. But one day there was an advertisement, a kid was in his band. Son Thomas was in the band playing the banjo, but he was drunk. The banjo was real important in a band without a piano. So, they had sat him in the corner, on the floor of the truck. It wasn't a truck, it was a horse and wagon, a furniture wagon. And they had sat him in the back next to the drums and they were playing without a banjo. So, an advertisement on the corner of Murray, Murray and Annette, I walked to the back of the truck and was looking to try to see the banjo. So, Alba Gannon was sitting on a tailgate, he and Marge French. So, Alba Gannon saw me with the ukulele and said, hey little Bob-A-Rant. He didn't know my name was Bob, he didn't know I was a Bob-A-Rant. He said, can you play banjo? I said, no. He said, come up here. So, I climbed up on a truck and sat down and said, can you play? I said, I don't think so. He said, well I'll tune it for you. So, he tuned it up for me, the ukulele style, you know. So, I sat in the band and played. And all the people, the second lines, was watching what was going on. I was like a hero. How old were you? About 14. So, I played that evening, I was like a hero. So, I played that evening with her. And I would have played that night. But my mother didn't think I should go and play at the hall, you know, too young. So, I did pretty good, at least, they thought. I guess I made up a lot of clinkers, you know, but nobody was annoyed as long as they heard that banjo. So, I had a reputation from that, see. The word passed around, old man Glenn, that this kid could be a wonderful banjo player if he had a banjo, you know. So, I got a letter from my uncle Paul and I told him what had happened. He said, I'll send you a banjo. He went back to Chicago. He was with King Oliver. So, he sent me a little small banjo. So, a little while, my little Boozanne King, I was playing the banjo with. So, there was Lawrence Turkel around town, a little Russell. Lawrence Turkel, a little Russell. We had a few rehearsals. We had a few rehearsals. We had a former little band. What did they play these guys? They were the same thing like, currently like, with what else. Lawrence Turkel. Lawrence Turkel played cornet. Lawrence Turkel played clarinet. And Russell played drum and banjo. Two horns. and Russell played drum and banjo, two horns, two of them, two, the boy in the street. We had a few rehearsals, and nothing happened because it was all, it was always, all afraid of the music and everything. So we just banded. So then I have an uncle called, my uncle's brother-in-law, who was Billy Phillips, he had a band. Called him Bigfoot Billy. He had some kind of serenaders. The Sunset or the Oriental Serenaders or something. So he sent for them and I joined his band. And he was very patient. He had a pretty good band. He used to play at the Lions Club, the Senators, and a lot of house parties, and a lot of white social affairs. He was a pretty good businessman. So I worked with his band for five or six months. All the time I'm improving. And then I, a guy came to my house and said, there's a band, Lee Collins and them need a band to play to go to Pensacola, Florida. Well, listen to that, that was later. I worked with gang of bands, dancing schools and different bands. You know, Willie Pajo's band. I worked with a guy then, can't think of his name. Never would pay you the money. Always fall out drunk and pay the time to come. Say, I see you Monday or something. Can't think of his name. And I worked with a lot of little groups around me. Around seventeen, I joined, Lee Collins' band. I went to Pensacola, Florida. Second day we were there, we found out we were stranded. Stayed there, I think, about two months. And I come back to New Orleans and I went on Alamo with Willie Pajo instead, I think. A year and a half.
